title: Beware of Saying "If You Got the Question Wrong, Make Sure You Have Corrected It"
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton recounts sitting beside a student during a lesson where the teacher went through test answers well — explaining clearly, taking input, checking for confusion — and still watched the student silently copy down a correct answer in green pen without understanding why it was right. When Barton asked the student to explain their mistake, they had no idea. He calls this the 'Myth of Copying Things Down': the physical act of writing a correct answer creates the appearance of learning on the page even though nothing has actually changed in the student's understanding, and a teacher scanning exercise books afterward can be completely misled by it. His fix is to treat copying down as, at most, the midpoint of the process rather than its conclusion — using a mini-whiteboard check beforehand to gauge how many students actually struggled, and a follow-up question of similar difficulty afterward to verify the correction actually took.
points: Barton names the 'Myth of Copying Things Down': the physical act of writing a correct answer in an exercise book looks like evidence of learning to a teacher scanning books later, even when no understanding changed.
His anecdote shows the failure mode concretely — a student silently copies a correct answer in green pen despite not understanding why the original method was wrong.
He is skeptical that a general instruction to 'ask if you're confused' catches most struggling students, since the only reason he caught this one was proximity, not the teacher's check.

His proposed fix has two checkpoints: gauge how many students struggled with the question in the first place (mini-whiteboards work well here), and follow the explanation with a similar-difficulty question that all students must answer to verify the correction actually landed.
quotes: The teacher did a really nice job of explaining to students how to do the questions, using a combination of asking students for input and supplementing this with her own explanations. After each solution, the teacher then asked if anyone was still confused or had any questions.
I asked the student if they could explain to me why they should have divided instead of multiplied. After a bit of mumbling, they explained that they didn’t have a clue.

Now, the only reason I picked up on this was because I was sitting next to the student at the time. How many other students had a similar lack of understanding? I had no idea, but more importantly, neither did the teacher.

Nothing magical happens during the act of copying an answer down from the board, and yet if the teacher looks at this sheet afterwards it will look like learning has taken place - the student didn’t understand before, and now they do.

If the teacher identifies that a significant number of students have struggled with this question - getting them all to copy their final answer onto a mini-whiteboard and show it to the teacher before she goes through the answers is a good way to do this - then after the explanation there needs to be a follow-up check for understanding.

This needs to be a question of similar difficulty that all students respond to - again our friend the mini-whiteboard is invaluable here - and if students get this question right, we can be much more confident that they are on the path to resolving their misunderstanding than if they simply whip out their green pens and copying things down off the board.
